# **Introduction to Xenium data**

***

Before we start to work with the Spatial Transcriptomics data from this study, we will provide an introduction previewing some of the specifics of Xenium data: how it's generated, what is produced or generally what you can expect working with it, and any special considerations to keep in mind when working with Xenium data. Some of these topics will be discussed in more detail throughout the case study.

## Data generation

Xenium is an image-based spatial transcriptomics platform. 

Cell segmentation for v1 utilizes DAPI for nucleus and an isotropic nuclear expansion algorithm to approximate the cell boundaries. An alternative approach (not used in the process of this paper) 



## Data products

## Summary

In Summary, Xenium data utilizes a gene panel of probes to assay the spatially-resolved expression of specific genes at a cellular or subcellular resolution within tissue samples. Samples used to generate Xenium data are either fresh frozen (FF) or formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue samples. After sample preparation, imaging cycles are performed using a Xenium Analyzer. Cellular segmentation is performed to approximate boundaries between cells.


# **What are the data?**

***

## Data context

***

The data used in this case study are from @Kwon_etal_2026 which collected dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) samples postmortem from neurotypical donors and donors with diagnosed schizophrenia. Samples were fresh frozen following collection prior to spatial transcriptomics dataset generation. @Kwon_etal_2026 generated data using both the Visium and Xenium platforms, using analysis of the Visium data to inform what Xenium data to collect. Visium data was generated for all donors as explained in [Supplementary Table 1](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/biorxiv/early/2026/05/23/2026.02.16.706214/DC2/embed/media-2.xlsx?download=true) while Xenium data was generated for a subset of these donors. For donors where both Visium and Xenium datasets were generated, the tissue samples originated from the same fresh frozen tissue block or source for each donor, but the samples themselves (used to generate the data for each platform) are from adjacent tissue sections of each block. Since each platform requires its own slide mounting and chemical reagents, typically serial tissue sectioning is used to yield adjacent / comparable tissue samples that can be used for multiple experiments with different technologies.

Postmortem tissue samples from 24 donors were used to generate Xenium data. Twelve of those donors had been diagnosed with schizophrenia (denoted by **SCZ** within the study and this case study) while the other 12 were neurotypical (denoted by *NTC* within the study and **CTRL** within this case study).

:::{.emphasis_block}
This case study will work solely with the Xenium data, using only 6 of the 24 samples (3 CTRL and 3 SCZ).
:::

We will work with a reduced number of samples in order to keep the size of the data more manageable. It's important, especially in studies involving visualization of tissue sections, to work with multiple tissue sections per case (e.g., CTRL vs SCZ) to make sure that signal is not an artifact of how that sample was processed or cut and instead is generalizable across tissue sections/samples.

<details><summary>Matching sample demographics</summary>

Typically studies match donor demographics between case cohorts (e.g., having comparable average ages or number of individuals of each sex). @Kwon_etal_2026 does this for all of the samples overall as well as the subset of samples that were processed with the Xenium platform, reporting the information in [Supplementary Table 1](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/biorxiv/early/2026/05/23/2026.02.16.706214/DC2/embed/media-2.xlsx?download=true).

</details>

:::{.emphasis_block}

The Xenium spatial transcriptomics data represents cellular mRNA counts for panel-targeted genes, mapping the transcripts from those genes to the cellular spatial locations in the tissue (where the probes bound, signifying expression). As such there are 3 main data types or files that we will be working with.

1. Tissue/sample metadata
2. Spatial coordinates of cells in the sample
3. mRNA counts of panel-targeted transcripts for each cell

:::

<details><summary>The panel genes</summary>

The panel targets 300 genes using probes designed specifically to target transcripts of these genes:

| Categories of gene used for the panel | Source                | Number of genes |
| :------------------------------------ | :-------------------: | :-------------: |
| Differentially expressed genes        | Visium data analysis in @Kwon_etal_2026 | 168 |
| dPFC Layer marker genes               | @Huuki-Myers_etal_2024 | 85 |
| Schizophrenia associated genes        | Various literature/GWAS studies (see [Supplementary Table 8](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/biorxiv/early/2026/05/23/2026.02.16.706214/DC9/embed/media-9.xlsx?download=true)) | 18 |
| Cell type marker genes                | @Huuki-Myers_etal_2024 | 35 |

Six genes (A2M, MAPK3, PLP1, RCAN2, SERPINA3, SOX2-OT) overlap multiple categories within the panel, leading to a total of 300 unique genes represented in the panel. An additional 68 genes already in the panel were also marked as cell type marker genes (beyond the original 35) following further literature review. This can be explored in [Supplementary Table 8](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/biorxiv/early/2026/05/23/2026.02.16.706214/DC9/embed/media-9.xlsx?download=true).

</details>

### Sample metadata

The sample metadata file that we will be working with combines the metadata from [Supplementary Table 1](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/biorxiv/early/2026/05/23/2026.02.16.706214/DC2/embed/media-2.xlsx?download=true) with the GEO accession number for each sample. When using secondary data, it is common for sample metadata to be available in supplementary information. You may need to combine multiple tables of information.

<details><summary> Expansion of metadata from Supplementary Table 1</summary>

We previously created a file for the Xenium samples which maps each sample's GEO Accession Number to the Brain Number ID (`geo_to_spatial_samples.csv`) and united this with the data from Supplementary Table 1 because we will need the GEO accession number in order to fetch the spatial coordaintes and mRNA counts for each sample. However, the sample metadata file provided in the supplementary table only includes the Brain Number ID (`Br####`). 

The files for this project follow the naming pattern of {sample specific GEO accession number}_{sample Brain Number ID}-{file type specific pattern},                       

* Listed files from GEO accession number GSE307404 (all Xenium data from this project) with `list.files()` function for one of the file types.
* Used `stringr::str_replace()` function to the specific pattern for that file type with an empty string (`""`), removing all but the GEO accession number and Brain Number ID (separated by an underscore) for each sample.
* Used `strsplit("_")` function to separate the GEO accession number and Brain Number ID for each string.
* Used `do.call(rbind.data.frame, .)` to create a data frame with the sample GEO accession numbers in the first column and their associated Brain Number IDs in the second column.
* Set the column names.
* Saved to a `.csv` file.

Alternatively, we could create this map using the `title` and `geo_accession` columns from the `pData(gse[[1]])` output we saw earlier.

</details>

The combined data from Supplementary Table 1 and the GEO to Brain Number ID map is contained in the file `spatial_samples.csv`. The `spatial_samples.csv` file is a file with a header (column names) where values are separated by a comma (`.csv`). The contents of each column are explained in the following table:

| Variable | Details |
|:-----------:|:-----------:|
| `BrainNumberID` | An identifier representing which donor brain the sample originates from. Follows the pattern "Br####" |
| `Race`          | Demographic information about donors. All samples are "CAUC" for caucasian. |
| `Sex`           | Demographic information about donors. "M" for male or "F" for female. |
| `Age`           | Demographic information about donors. Number / decimal representing age of donor in years. |
| `RIN`           | RNA Integrity Number. Number / decimal representing the quality of the fresh frozen block tissue samples. Generally, [Visium](https://cdn.10xgenomics.com/image/upload/v1726523282/support-documents/CG000763_VisiumHDFFTissuePrepHandbook_RevA_1.pdf) and [Xenium recommend](https://kb.10xgenomics.com/s/article/34005267962125-What-should-I-consider-when-processing-Human-Brain-on-Xenium) brain tissues have an observed RIN of 4+ (though older resources may recommend 7+) (@Grases_Porta-Pardo_2026). Lower RINs may lead to reduced sensitivity. |
| `PMI`           | Postemortem Interval. Number / decimal representing the time interval between the donor's death and the sample extraction and freezing from that donor. Typically reported in hours, but could be reported in days or another measurement of time. To promote greater fresh frozen block tissue quality, generally it is recommended to [minimize the post mortem interval](https://cdn.10xgenomics.com/image/upload/v1726523282/support-documents/CG000763_VisiumHDFFTissuePrepHandbook_RevA_1.pdf) |
| `PrimaryDx`     | Demographic information about donors representing the primary diagnosis. "Control" for neurotypical donors and "Schizophrenia" for donors diagnosed with schizophrenia. | 
| `Visium`        | "YES" or "NO" for whether Visium data was generated for this sample. All samples are "YES". |
| `Xenium`        | "YES" or "NO" for whether Xenium data was generated for this sample. |
| `GEO`           | The GEO accession number for samples with Xenium data. NA for samples with only Visium data. |

The demographic information is useful for data exploration. We will primarily be using the `BrainNumberID`, `PrimaryDx`, `Xenium`, and `GEO` variables. 

* The `Xenium` and `GEO` variables will be used to select a subset of samples of fetch the data for those samples from GEO. 
* The `BrainNumberID` and `PrimaryDx` variables will be used to create informative sample IDs so that we can more easily observe the case (e.g., CTRL or SCZ) of samples throughout our analysis.
 
### Spatial coordinates

Classically, `-cells.parquet` files are used to store the spatial coordinates of the cells, specifically the {{ < glossary Centroid display=centroid > }} locations (or centers of the cells).

The `.parquet` file type is a departure from the normal way we would expect data to be stored. Often our file types (e.g., `.csv`) store data row by row with each row containing a complete record or set of related information about a specific sample, timepoint, etc. Instead, `.parquet` files store data column-by-column. This leads to more efficient storage and querying of large data files.

Additional information provided in this file is [described by 10X genomics](https://www.10xgenomics.com/support/software/xenium-onboard-analysis/latest/analysis/xoa-output-understanding-outputs#cell-summary).

<details><summary>If `-cells.parquet` files are not available</summary>

Sometimes when you are using publicly available data rather than generating new datasets yourself, files that you may expect are not deposited or archived. 

If `.parquet` files are not available, first check if `cells.csv.gz` is available as this is an alternate format of the typical file. If not, you can use a different Xenium output to calculate the centroids typically stored in the `cells.parquet` files. This will be explored further within a click to expand section in the [Data Import](https://www.opencasestudies.org/ocs-bio-spatial-transcriptomics/#data-import) section of the case study, but this alternate file type is also introduced here:

`-cell_boundaries.csv.gz` also stores spatial coordinates. Specifically these files have many rows per cell describing each vertex that is part of a polygon, where the polygon edges represent the borders of the cell. We can find the centroid of each cell by considering all of these polygon coordinates together. The contents of this file are the result of the nucleus segmentation algorithm that expands the nuclei DAPI-stained boundaries to determine cell boundaries.

| Variable | Details |
| :-------: | :----------------------:|
| `cell_id` | A cell ID corresponding to the `barcode` variable in the mRNA counts data. Multiple rows will have the same `cell_id` value in these files. |
| `vertex_x`| The x-coordinate of a vertex between two of the edges of the polygon representing that cell. |
| `vertex_y`| The corresponding y-coordinate of that vertex between two of the edges of the polygon representing that cell. |


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html//1jRNbuvQSjI4cZKAOStDUFAgAoFFBp8zIICCiG-1RZLk_h6a9b871c28945653_0_0.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Illustration showing how centroid coordinates can be found for a polygon with vertex coordinates and the format by which the data is provided from Xenium.' width=100%}
:::
:::


Another file output that Xenium provides is `nucleus_boundaries`. This file is not sufficient for cell spatial coordinates because it's only providing the boundaries of the nucleus rather than the cells. Nuclear positioning varies across cells, so you can't make an assumption about the center of cell if you have coordinates for the nucleus. 

These file types are described in greater [detail by 10X genomics](https://www.10xgenomics.com/support/software/xenium-onboard-analysis/latest/analysis/xoa-output-understanding-outputs#segmentation).

</details>

:::{.emphasis_block}
This case study will use the `arrow` package to work with `-cells.parquet` files for the spatial coordinates data. 
:::

### mRNA counts

The data for the mRNA counts that we'll be using is stored in `-cell_feature_matrix.h5` files. This file type efficiently stores large amounts of data that are typically represented by large matrices (n rows for genes * m columns for cells with counts for a given gene in a specific cell stored at each intersection). Instead, `.h5` files use nested named lists to store the data. Of important note, only non-zero counts are stored as well as the indices where those counts would be located in a matrix (e.g., indices for which genes and cell IDs they would correspond with). These nested named lists can be used to reconstruct the matrix structure of the data. 

Note that "features" is an alternative word for genes in this field and will be used interchangeably throughout this case study.

We can use either the `rhdf5::h5dump()` function or the `rhdf5::h5ls()` function to get a look at the nested lists (and their names) for this data.

```{.r .cell-code}
decompress_read_parquet <- function(samples_metadata, sample){
  #Build file paths
  gz_file <- here(paste0("data/raw/",
                         sample,
                         "/",
                         sample,
                         "_",
                         samples_metadata[which(samples_metadata$sampleID == sample), "brainNumID"],
                         "-cells.parquet.gz"))
  
  decompressed_file <- str_replace(gz_file, ".gz", "")

  #Decompress
  R.utils::gunzip(gz_file, destname = decompressed_file, remove = FALSE, skip = TRUE)

  #Read in
  df <- arrow::read_parquet(decompressed_file)

  #Remove the decompressed file because we no longer need it
  file.remove(decompressed_file)
  
  #Select columns of interest
  centroids <- df %>%
    select(cell_id, x_centroid, y_centroid)

  #reclaim some R resources
  rm(df, gz_file, decompressed_file)
  gc()

  #Return
  return(centroids)

}
```

```{.r .cell-code}
read_rna <- function(samples_metadata, sample){

  h5file <- here(paste0("data/raw/",
                         sample,
                         "/",
                         sample,
                         "_",
                         samples_metadata[which(samples_metadata$sampleID == sample), "brainNumID"],
                        "-cell_feature_matrix.h5"))
                              

  rna_h5data <- rhdf5::h5read(h5file, name = "matrix")

  rna_mat <- Matrix::sparseMatrix(i = rna_h5data$indices,
                       p = rna_h5data$indptr,
                       x = as.integer(rna_h5data$data),
                       dims = rna_h5data$shape,
                       index1 = FALSE) %>%
      as.matrix() %>%
      as.data.frame() %>%
      `rownames<-`(rna_h5data$features$name) %>%
      `colnames<-`(rna_h5data$barcodes) %>%
      rownames_to_column("genes")

  rm(rna_h5data, h5file)
  gc()

  return(rna_mat)
}
```

## Filtering

### Using Control Probes and Codewords

First we create a function that we can use with lapply that takes the filtering thresholds that we found previously as well as the counts matrix as inputs. Notice that the thresholds are named arguments meaning they have default values set to the exact variables we were working with earlier. We find the combined expression within each cell of each of the three associated controls using column sums and identify the cell IDs where the combined expression of any one of these types of controls is greater than or equal to the 99th percentile threshold. Finally, we take a union of the identified cell IDs.

By calling this function with `lapply`, we'll have named list (`to_remove_all`) where the sample name stores a vector of cell IDs that should be removed for that sample.

We use a `for` loop to then loop through the sample names and actually filter the cell IDs within the count matrix. Recall that the cells correspond to the columns in the count matrix. Our filter is specifically using an exclamation point (`!`) to specify that if a column name is **not** the list of cell IDs to be filtered, then keep it.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
findOverlap <- function(mat, negcp = negcontrol_probe_cutoff, negcc = negcontrol_cdwd_cutoff, ucc = unassigned_cdwd_cutoff){
    which_negcp <- names(which(mat[startsWith(rownames(mat), "NegControlProbe"), ] %>% Matrix::colSums() >= negcp))
    which_negcc <- names(which(mat[startsWith(rownames(mat), "NegControlCodeword"), ] %>% Matrix::colSums() >= negcc))
    which_ucc <- names(which(mat[startsWith(rownames(mat), "Unassigned"), ] %>% Matrix::colSums() >= ucc))

    to_remove <- union(union(which_negcp, which_negcc), which_ucc)

    return(to_remove)
}

to_remove_all <- lapply(scz_spatial@counts, function(x) findOverlap(x))

for (sample_name in names(to_remove_all)){
    scz_spatial@counts[[sample_name]] <- scz_spatial@counts[[sample_name]][,!colnames(scz_spatial@counts[[sample_name]]) %in% to_remove_all[[sample_name]]]
}
```

```{.r .cell-code}
            data.frame() %>% 
            rownames_to_column("libname")
    ) %>% `colnames<-`(c("libname", "annot", sample_name))
}

use_combined_data <- function(mat, gene_name, use = "violin", samples = c("Br1139SCZ", "Br5314CTRL")){
  combined_data <- bind_rows(combine_counts_annot(mat@spatial_meta, mat@tr_counts, samples[1], gene_name),
                             combine_counts_annot(mat@spatial_meta, mat@tr_counts, samples[2], gene_name)) %>%
                      pivot_longer(starts_with("Br"),
                                   values_to = "tr_counts",
                                   names_to = "sample") %>%
                      drop_na()

  if (use == "violin"){
    return(
      combined_data %>%
        ggplot(aes(x = sample, 
               y = tr_counts, 
               fill = sample)) + 
        geom_violin() + 
        facet_wrap(~annot, scales = "free_y") + 
        theme_bw() + 
        scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.6) + 
        ggtitle(gene_name) +
        theme(legend.position = "bottom")
    )
  } else if (use == "summary"){
    table_length <- length(unique(combined_data$annot)) * 2
    return(
      combined_data %>%
        group_by(annot, sample) %>% 
        summarize(
              min_exp = min(tr_counts), 
              max_exp = max(tr_counts), 
              avg_exp = mean(tr_counts),
              median_exp = median(tr_counts),
              var_exp = var(tr_counts)
        ) %>% 
    print(n=table_length)
    )
  } else {
    message("No other downstream uses supported besides 'violin' and 'summary'")
  }
}
```
